w:r.w:t: This policy sets out how the firm selects, approves, monitors and exits third party arrangements. It applies to every arrangement under which a third party performs a process, service or activity that the firm would otherwise undertake itself, and to every arrangement that supports an important business service.
The policy is owned by the Chief Risk Officer and approved by the Board. It is reviewed annually, and out of cycle whenever a material change to the firm’s outsourcing footprint occurs.
An arrangement is outsourcing where all three of the following hold:
The activity is one the firm could perform itself.
The activity is performed on a recurring or continuous basis.
The activity supports a regulated activity or an important business service.
An arrangement that fails any of the three is a supplier arrangement rather than an outsourcing arrangement, and is governed by the procurement standard instead.
The purchase of goods that are not services.
Correspondent banking relationships, which are governed separately.
Intra-group arrangements, which follow the intra-group services framework.

The Board retains accountability for every outsourced activity. Accountability cannot be delegated to a third party, and the firm remains responsible to its customers and its regulators for the outcome of anything it outsources.
Approves the policy and any critical arrangement
Reviews the register and the concentration analysis

Every arrangement in scope is recorded in the outsourcing register. The register holds, for each arrangement, the provider, the service, the criticality assessment, the contract dates, the exit plan reference, and the name of the individual accountable for it.

Due diligence is proportionate to criticality. A critical arrangement requires the full assessment set out below; a non-critical arrangement requires the financial and information security assessments alone.
Financial standing, covering at least three years of accounts.
Information security, including a review of the provider’s certifications and the results of the most recent independent assessment.
Operational resilience, covering the provider’s own impact tolerances and its dependency on further sub-outsourcing.
Regulatory standing, including any enforcement history in the jurisdictions in which the provider operates.
Concentration, both the firm’s concentration on the provider and the provider’s concentration across the sector.

A provider may not sub-outsource a material part of a critical service without the firm’s prior written consent. The contract must give the firm the right to object, and a reasonable period in which to exercise it.
Every contract for a critical arrangement carries, as a minimum:
A clear description of the service and the service levels attached to it.
Audit and access rights for the firm, its auditors and its regulators.
Data location and data processing terms.
Termination rights, including for a change of control.
A transition-out obligation lasting at least the exit plan’s stated period.

Service levels are reported monthly to the service owner and quarterly to the Risk Committee. A breach that persists for two consecutive reporting periods is escalated to the Outsourcing Forum, whatever its severity.
Service owner, within one business day
Outsourcing Forum, at its next meeting

Every critical arrangement carries a documented and tested exit plan. The plan names the trigger events, the target state, the sequence of steps, the resources required, and the period over which the exit would run.
An exit plan that has never been tested is a document rather than a plan. Each critical exit plan is tested at least once every two years, and the test result is reported to the Risk Committee.
An arrangement is critical where its failure would materially impair an important business service, breach a regulatory obligation, or cause material detriment to customers.
A service delivered to an external end user, the disruption of which could cause intolerable harm
The maximum tolerable disruption to an important business service
A provider’s own outsourcing of part of the service it supplies to the firm
